passage:
Thursday night
Today was the class trip to the botanical garden. On the rocky path near the lotus pond, Reena tripped and fell on her knee. It was bleeding a lot. Two girls screamed and one boy ran off.
My tummy went jumpy. I felt really sorry for her because her face was all crumpled. But I made my breathing slow, like we do in yoga, and said, "Reena, stay here. I'm getting Miss."
I walked fast, not ran, because the path was slippery. Miss D'Souza was near the bus. I told her, "Reena fell by the pond, her knee is bleeding." She grabbed the first-aid bag and I showed her the way.
Miss cleaned it, put on a big bandage and said, "Good boy, Joseph." Reena said thank you to me on the bus.
Joseph

In September, Rimjhim's older brother was in a bad bike accident and was in hospital for weeks. Rimjhim is Bidisha's closest friend. For the first fortnight Bidisha was her rock. She stayed on the phone with her till late, went to the hospital after school, cried with her in the washroom.
Then Bidisha started coming in with dark circles, yawning through physics. She fell asleep in the library once. She stopped eating her tiffin.
By October, something flipped. When Rimjhim walked toward our bench, Bidisha suddenly needed to go to the staff room. Her phone buzzed and she turned it over without looking. I asked her if they'd fought. She said, "No. I just can't. I'm so tired." Her eyes filled up.
I don't know everything she was feeling. But she didn't look like someone who stopped caring.

passage:
Supervision note, Thursday. Damini Rao, clinical supervisor, counselling practicum.
Tanvir (21, final-year student) asked to speak after group. For his first two months at the community clinic he stayed late after every session, and twice told me he cried on the bus home. This month is different. He described sitting with a mother whose son had run away and feeling "nothing, like a wall." Afterwards he snapped at the receptionist over a file.
He asked me, very quietly, "Have I stopped caring? Maybe I'm not made for this." He looked ashamed.
I told him the flatness he describes often comes after feeling too much for too long, and that it is a sign of fatigue, not of a missing heart. Next steps: his caseload cut from six to four for three weeks, a ten-minute pause between sessions, and a weekly check-in with me. I will ask how he is sleeping.

qa.q: What did Tanvir snap at the receptionist about?
qa.a: He snapped at the receptionist over a file.

qa.a: He believed his numbness meant he had lost his kindness, and that frightened him because he wants to be a good counsellor.

qa.a: Damini named his flatness as fatigue and cut his caseload, added pauses and weekly check-ins, which gives him room to recover instead of pushing on until he quits.

qa.q: How might the receptionist have experienced Tanvir's snapping?

subtype: Caring role wears the carer down [Actor]
passage:
Wednesday night
Child ward again today. A little girl screamed through her whole drip change, and I just held her arm and did it. Felt nothing. Not sad, not sorry, nothing. In first year I cried in the locker room over a boy who wanted his Ammi.
Then Harish called during dinner to tell me about his cricket team, and I snapped, "Can you not talk for five minutes?" My little brother. He just said "okay, Didi" and hung up.
I lay on the hostel bed thinking maybe I'm a hard person now. Maybe I chose the wrong course.
But I remember Ma'am in our psych lecture talking about compassion fatigue: people who feel too much for too long can go numb. That's literally me. It isn't that my heart is gone. It's that it's tired.
Tomorrow: say sorry to Harish, sleep before eleven, and ask Sister Mercy if I can talk to her.
Parul

Preeti was halfway through her coffee at the co-working space in Indiranagar when Jagdish, from the next desk, put his phone down and went grey. "They've let me go. Just an email. Eight of us."
His hands were shaking. Preeti felt her own chest tighten, as if the email had been hers too. She set the cup down, let out a long slow breath, then another, and felt her shoulders drop.
"That's awful, Jagdish," she said, and meant it. "What would help right now? Air? Someone to sit with you? Or should I call someone?"
"Just... sit for a bit."
So she sat. Later she walked with him to the auto stand and messaged to check he got home.
That night she wanted to keep texting him till midnight. Instead she sent one message, "Here tomorrow if you want to talk," and went to bed early. She had a long week ahead, and he would need her in it.

"Sabina, beti, you keep saying 'fine' to your mother. Let your Bhupen Mama tell you something.
When I was fifteen in Tezpur, my own mother asked me every evening, 'How was school?' 'Fine.' 'Why are you so quiet?' 'Nothing.' That was my whole vocabulary. And I wasn't lying. I truly didn't know what else to say.
But my body knew. My neck hurt, my stomach hurt before exams, I got headaches every Sunday night. I told the school nurse about the aches, never about anything else, because there was no anything else I could find.
Years later I realised I had been frightened of failing, and lonely after my best friend changed schools. I didn't have the words. I had a stiff neck instead.
So when you say 'fine' and then complain about your back, I don't think you're cold, Sabina. I think you're like me at fifteen."

Sabina had been married to Bhupen for a year when her mother fell ill in the next town. Bhupen shut his tea stall in Nalbari for two days, drove her to the hospital on his scooter, and sat in the corridor all night. He never once said he was worried. When she cried, he handed her a bottle of water.
Back home, she watched him wiping the stall counter, slowly, the same spot again and again.
"Do you feel anything?" she asked. "About Ma, about me? You never say."
Bhupen kept wiping. "I closed the stall."
"That's not what I asked."
He stopped. His ears were red. "I don't know how to say it like you do," he mumbled.
Sabina felt a sharp mix of hurt and something softer. She had heard coldness for a year. She looked at the scooter parked outside, still dusty from the hospital road.

I'm Parveen. I sit across from Ujjwal at the bank branch, and this spring I noticed changes.
First there was a sticky note on the side of his monitor, a list of words in tiny writing: annoyed, let down, uneasy, relieved, left out. When he finished a hard call, I'd see him glance at it.
Then, during a tense meeting with the regional manager, he put his hand flat on his chest for a moment, breathed, and wrote something in a small brown notebook. He writes in that notebook every day at lunch too, a few lines.
One evening, walking to the metro, he told me, "My fiancée said I'm hard to reach. I realised I couldn't tell her what I felt, even to myself. So I see a counsellor on Thursdays now."
I don't know what's in the notebook. But last week, when I said I was stressed, he said, "Uneasy or overwhelmed?" and actually listened to the answer.

qa.q: What words were on the sticky note on Ujjwal's monitor?
qa.a: Annoyed, let down, uneasy, relieved, left out.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's hand on his chest suggest he was feeling in the tense meeting?
qa.a: It suggests he felt tense or uneasy and was using the feeling in his chest as a clue, pausing to name it in his notebook.

qa.q: What choice set Ujjwal's changes in motion, and why does it matter?
qa.a: After his fiancée said he was hard to reach, he chose to see a counsellor and practise with a word list and notebook, turning a hurt into steady learning.

qa.q: How has Ujjwal's effort affected Parveen?
qa.a: Parveen now gets a colleague who asks 'uneasy or overwhelmed?' and listens, so Parveen feels more understood at work.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, an adult who builds a list of feeling words, notices body cues, writes daily notes and sees a counsellor because the difficulty was hurting his relationship.

passage:
Week one. Jahnavi, his sister, had asked Akash why he never said how he felt, and he couldn't answer. So he downloaded a feelings chart and stuck it inside his wardrobe. Most words looked the same to him. The only thing he could write in his phone notes that night was: "Chest tight before meeting."
Week three. At his second session, the counsellor asked what the tight chest might be. Akash stared at the chart printout. "Nervous? No. Scared I'll look stupid." He was surprised by how right it felt.
Week seven. Sunday lunch at their parents' flat. Everyone was planning Jahnavi's engagement, and nobody had asked him anything. Akash put his fork down. "I feel left out," he said. "I'd like to help with something."
Jahnavi stared at him, then grinned. "Who are you, and what have you done with my brother?" She handed him the guest list.

qa.q: Where did Akash stick the feelings chart?
qa.a: He stuck it inside his wardrobe.

qa.q: Why was Akash surprised in week three?
qa.a: He was surprised because naming the tight chest as being scared he'll look stupid felt so right, after weeks when all the words looked the same.

qa.q: What was the turning point at Sunday lunch, and how did it change things?
qa.a: Akash chose to say 'I feel left out' and ask to help, instead of staying silent, and Jahnavi responded by giving him the guest list.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see the change in her brother?
qa.a: She is surprised and pleased, and her joke shows that hearing him name a feeling is new and welcome after she once asked why he never did.

grounding: It shows an adult who learns feeling words over weeks with a chart, notes on body cues and a counsellor, until he can say what he feels to his family.
